<reason>A built a tighter, more damaging chain of argument. By forcing B to clarify that "priority booking" operates inside an unchanged conservation cap, A extracted the pivotal concession in B4.1 that resident priority produces "no physical effect" on the fragile site — undercutting the motion's own framing around "fragile heritage sites." A then converted B's own numbers (a 10-20% resident quota) into a devastating comparative: a levy-funded cap benefits every resident with money and equal access to a fair lottery, while B's mechanism still excludes 80-90% of residents identically to a plain cap, and does so by either cutting conservation revenue or regressively surcharging modest-income visitors. B's distributive-justice reframe (permanent steward vs. transient extractive visitor) is a coherent value claim, but B never neutralizes A's quantification critique or the eligibility-scope paradox (broad enough to include commuters dilutes the quota to meaninglessness; narrow enough to be meaningful excludes the workers B wants to protect). B's honest concession on "no physical effect" is admirable epistemically but rhetorically costly, since it hands A the cleanest closing line. Both sides executed the format cleanly (Q1/Q2, A1/A2), but A's rebuttals did more real damage round over round.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A's Pressure Question Q1 ("name one physical effect... that the conservation cap does not already produce") and B's honest but costly concession in A1 of Rebuttal 2 ("No physical effect — and I won't pretend otherwise") was the decisive exchange: it handed A the framing for the entire closing round.</best_rebuttal>
